independence_day.intro: Finland celebrates Independence Day on 6 December. The occasion combines national pride with a quiet winter atmosphere of candles, flags and remembrance.
independence_day.history: On 6 December 1917, Finland’s parliament approved the declaration of independence from Russia. The date became the national celebration of Finnish independence. Commemorations also honour those who defended the country and helped build its society.
independence_day.traditions: Many homes place two candles in a window in the evening. Flags are raised, services and memorial ceremonies are held, and students take part in torchlight processions. The President’s Independence Day reception is widely watched on television.
funFacts: The date falls during Finland’s dark winter season, giving candles a special place in the celebrations.
The presidential reception is commonly called Linnan juhlat, the Castle Ball.

midsummer_day.intro: Juhannus, Finnish Midsummer, celebrates the light-filled summer season. Midsummer Day falls on the Saturday between 20 and 26 June, with many celebrations beginning on the Friday evening.
midsummer_day.history: Older midsummer customs became associated with the Christian feast of John the Baptist, from whose name Juhannus derives. Finland moved the observance from a fixed 24 June to its present Saturday rule in 1955. Today it is a major occasion for family gatherings and time in nature.
midsummer_day.traditions: Many people head to lakeside cottages, heat the sauna and share meals outdoors. Birch branches decorate doorways, and bonfires are lit where local conditions and fire restrictions permit. Dances and evenings by the water are also part of the tradition.
funFacts: Juhannus is also Finland’s Flag Day.
For Midsummer, flags traditionally remain flying through the night.
The midnight sun is visible in northern Finland; farther south, summer nights are still very light.
